title: Retirement confusion fuels calls for super and pension integration
full_text:
Australians are struggling to navigate the retirement system, with new research commissioned by Rest finding many members are unsure how superannuation and the Age Pension work together and calling for closer integration between the two.
The survey found 43 per cent of Rest members were unaware what steps they needed to take to prepare for retirement, while 61 per cent supported greater integration between super funds and Centrelink to simplify access to the Age Pension.
Government figures cited by Rest showed 2.7 million Australians aged 65 and over relied on the Age Pension, including around two-thirds receiving the full-rate pension and one-third receiving a part pension.
Additionally, the fund pointed to research showing almost one in three Age Pension recipients delayed lodging an application by more than a year, suggesting many retirees continued to find the system difficult to navigate.
Rest chief executive, Vicki Doyle, said the findings highlighted a growing disconnect in Australia’s retirement system.
“Superannuation and the Age Pension are meant to work together, but too often people are left trying to bridge the gap between them.
“When people don’t know what steps to take as they approach retirement, it’s a warning sign that the two biggest parts of Australia’s retirement system aren’t working together as seamlessly as they should.”
Members aged between 46 and 66 were the most likely to describe the retirement system as complex, indicating confusion peaked as people approached retirement.
The research also found women were significantly more likely than men to feel unsure about preparing for retirement and more likely to find retirement products difficult to understand.
Renters were among the least-prepared groups, with almost two in three saying they were unclear about how to prepare for retirement, compared with around one in three homeowners.
Doyle said the findings pointed to broader shortcomings in the design of the retirement system rather than simply a lack of consumer education.
“If Australians find the retirement system hardest to navigate at the point they need it most, that’s not simply a consumer education issue – it’s a system design issue.
“People shouldn’t have to become experts in superannuation, the Age Pension and Centrelink just to plan for retirement.
“Australians need a retirement system that feels like one connected experience, with simpler pathways and better integration between the services they rely on most,” Doyle said.
Rest said the challenges facing renters were expected to become more significant as more Australians retired without owning their home outright.
Furthermore, the fund noted higher housing costs could leave retirees increasingly reliant on both superannuation and the Age Pension, while older women remained particularly vulnerable to housing insecurity and homelessness.
The findings align with Rest’s 2026–27 pre-Budget submission, which calls for stronger integration between superannuation and the Age Pension, improved information sharing between government agencies and super funds, and progress on the Delivering Better Financial Outcomes advice reforms.
Rest said it had also invested in digital tools, including its Rest Retire Ready platform, to help members prepare for retirement with tailored guidance and support.
